512:3. Global Sections
513-
514-We shall now show how the structures we have exposed in our mathematical description of
515:empirical models can be brought to bear on the analysis of non-locality and contextuality.
516-
517-      We have already observed that the presheaf of events E is in fact a sheaf; it is natural to ask
518:if the same holds for the presheaf DRE. Indeed, since empirical models are compatible families for
519-this presheaf, to say that the sheaf condition holds for such a family {eC}CM, with respect to a
520:measurement cover M, is to say that there exists a global section d  DRE(X), defined on the
521:entire set of measurements X. Such a global section defines a distribution on the set E(X) = OX ,
522-which specifies assignments of outcomes to all measurements. Moreover, this distribution must
523:restrict to yield the probabilities specified by the empirical model on all the measurement contexts
524:in M: i.e. for all C  M, d|C = eC. Thus the existence of a global section for the empirical
525-model corresponds exactly to the existence of a distribution defined on all measurements, which
526-marginalizes to yield the empirically observed probabilities. This places the idea of extendability
527-of probability distributions, as studied in pioneering work by Fine [22], in a canonical and general
528-mathematical form.
529-
530:      We can say more than this. A global assignment s  E(X) = OX , i.e. a global section of
531-the sheaf E, can be seen as a canonical form of deterministic hidden variable, which assigns
532-a definite outcome to each measurement, independent of the measurement context in which it
533:appears. This yields an assignment s|C for each measurement context C. A global section
534-d  DRE(X) specifies a distribution on this canonical set of deterministic hidden variables. Each
535-s  OX induces a distribution s  DRE(X), where s(s) = 1, and s(s) = 0 if s = s. The
536-distribution induced by s on each measurement context C is s|C; note that s|C = s|C . Now we
537-have:
--
564-
565-      We can summarize this discussion as follows:
566-The Sheaf-Theoretic Structure Of Non-Locality and Contextuality                 10
567-
568:Proposition 3.1 The existence of a global section for an empirical model implies the existence
569-of a local (or non-contextual) deterministic hidden-variable model which realizes it.¶
570-
571-      We note also that, as we shall show later (see Theorem 8.1), apparently more general forms
572:of realization of empirical models by factorizable hidden-variable models, in which the hidden
573-variables are not required to be deterministic, are in fact equivalent to canonical realizations
574:by global sections. Thus the entire issue of non-locality and contextuality -- i.e. the existence of
575:empirical models which have no such realizations -- is equivalently formulated as the non-existence
576:of global sections for the corresponding compatible families.
577-
578-      Thus we have a characterization of the phenomena of locality and non-contextuality in terms of
579:obstructions to the existence of global sections, a central issue in the pervasive applications
580-of sheaves in geometry, topology, analysis and number theory. This opens the door to the use of
581-the powerful methods of sheaf theory in the study of non-locality and contextuality.

584-

586-

588-
589-We shall give a general linear-algebraic method for answering this question, which as we have
590-seen is equivalent to the question of whether there exists a realization of the model by local or
591-non-contextual hidden variables.

772:4.3. Global Sections as Solutions of Linear Systems
773-
774:Now we consider an empirical model {eC}, defined with respect to the distribution functor DR.
775-Such a model assigns a weight in the semiring R to each section si  E(C). Thus it can be specified
776-by a vector V of length p, where V[i] = eC (si). We can also introduce a vector X of length q of
777:`unknowns', one for each global section tj  E(X). Now a solution for the linear system MX = V
778-will be a vector of values in R, one for each tj. To ensure that this vector is a distribution, we
779-augment M with an extra row, every entry in which is 1, and similarly augment V with an extra
780-element, also set to 1. A solution for this augmented system will enforce the constraint

786-for each section sj.

901:extendable it it has no global section over DR0 , and possibilistically non-extendable if its
902:support has no global section over DB. We have seen that possibilistic non-extendability is strictly
903-stronger than probabilistic non-extendability.
904-
905-5. Negative Probabilities
906-
907-We shall now consider the question of extendability over real-valued distributions DR, i.e. signed
908-probability measures. Formally, this simply amounts to solving the linear system over the
909-reals, with no additional constraints. Conceptually, this allows the introduction of negative
910-probabilities in the extended model. Of course, these marginalize to yield standard non-negative
911:probabilities in the measurement contexts stipulated by the empirical model. Thus the usual
912-relative-frequency interpretation of the actually observed statistics is maintained.
913-
914-      The appearance of negative probabilities in quantum mechanics has a long history, which we
915:shall sketch in the Postlude (Section 10). In this section, we shall prove that all empirical models
916-are extendable with respect to signed probability measures. In fact, there is an equivalence between
917:extendability under signed measures and no-signalling. Note that the class of no-signalling models
918:is strictly larger than the empirical models of this type that arise in quantum mechanics. For
919-example, it includes the superquantum Popescu-Rohrlich boxes [10].
920-
921-      The result therefore shows that negative probabilities, in themselves, cannot characterize
922-quantum mechanics. This runs contrary to an impression which might be gained from the
923-literature. For example, Feynman writes: "The only difference between a probabilistic classical
924-world and the equations of the quantum world is that somehow or other it appears as if the
925-probabilities would have to go negative . . . " [26, p. 480]. In fact, the introduction of negative
926:probabilities yields the entire no-signalling world.
927-
928-5.1. Solving the Linear System Over the Reals
929-
930:Given an empirical model e over DR, our aim is to find a global section. The existence of such
931:a global section for e, which is represented by the real vector V, reduces to the existence of a
932-solution for the linear system MX = V over the reals, with no additional constraints.
933-
934:      Note that there is no semiring homomorphism from the reals to the booleans. Indeed, if there
935:were such a homomorphism h, we would have:
936-
937-                     0 = h(0) = h(1 + (-1)) = h(1)  h(-1) = 1  h(-1) = 1.
938-The Sheaf-Theoretic Structure Of Non-Locality and Contextuality         15
939-
940:A similar argument shows that there is no homomorphism from the reals to the non-negative reals.
941-Thus there is no result analogous to Proposition 4.4, and it is possible for the linear system to be
942-solvable over the reals, while no solution exists over the non-negative reals or the booleans.
943-
944:      We shall now show that such solutions exist for all no-signalling probabilistic empirical models,
945:over arbitrary measurement covers. This substantially generalizes previous results, e.g. Theorem 1

1448-7.1. Kochen-Specker Graphs
1449-
1450:The measurement covers which can be represented by quantum systems are of a particular form:
1451-they are generated by a symmetric binary compatibility relation, since compatibility in
1452-quantum mechanics means that the observables pairwise commute. Thus, for example, the
1453-`triangle' cannot arise from quantum observables.
1454-
--
1456-directly to some standard notions in graph theory.
1457-
1458-      An undirected graph G is specified by a finite set of vertices VG, and a set of edges EG, which
1459-are two-element subsets of VG. A clique of G is a set C  VG with an edge between every pair of
1460:vertices in C. The set of maximal cliques of G forms a measurement cover MG.
1461-
1462-      Let G be a graph. A set S  VG is called a stable transversal [36] if for every maximal
1463-clique C of G (i.e. for every C  MG), |S  C| = 1. Note that it is necessarily the case that a
1464-stable transversal is independent, i.e. there is no edge between any pair of elements of S, since
1465-otherwise we could extend this pair to a maximal clique containing both.

1648-9. Quantum Representations
1649-
1650-Since our aim is to investigate general properties of systems and physical theories, it has
--
1654-
1655-      However, it is important to make explicit how the structures we have described can be
1656-represented in quantum mechanics.
1657-
1658:      We begin with measurement covers. A quantum representation of a measurement cover on
1659-a set X can be described as follows. We fix a Hilbert space H. As usual, an observable is a
1660-bounded self-adjoint operator A on H. Two observables A, B are compatible if they commute:
1661-AB = BA. In this case, the composite AB is again self-adjoint, and hence forms an observable.
1662-
1663:      Given a set X = {Ax}xX of observables on H indexed by X, we form a measurement cover by
1664-taking M to be the set of all maximal commuting subsets of X . Note that pairwise commutation
1665-implies that the observables in each such subset, composed in any order, form a well-defined
1666:observable. We say that an abstract measurement cover M has a quantum representation if
1667-it arises in this way.
1668-
1669-      For Bell-type scenarios, a quantum representation will have a particular form, reflecting the
1670-usual idea that the measurements are performed at a number of different sites, which may be
1671-space-like separated. We will have a family {Hi} of Hilbert spaces, one for each part. The
1672-elements of Xi will index a family Xi of incompatible (i.e. non-commuting) observables on Hi. We
1673-make these into local observables on the compound system H = H1  · · ·  Hk, by defining
1674-Ai := I  · · ·  A  · · ·  I for each A  Xi. Then Ai commutes with Bj whenever i = j, and we
1675:can form a measurement cover of Bell type on the compound system.

1740-family? In the case of a Bell-type scenario, the fact that they do is the content of the standard
1741:no-signalling theorem [17]. However, Bell-type scenarios are very special cases of measurement
1742-covers. We shall therefore verify explicitly that the distributions determined by a quantum state,

1776-compatible families of observables in general, not just those represented as operating on different
1777:factors of a tensor product. This form of no-signalling says that, at the level of distributions, the
1778-statistics obtained for a measurement on a given state are independent of the context of other
1779-compatible measurements which may also have been performed.

1784-can represent these two sets of observables as acting on different factors of a tensor product. The
1785:standard version of no-signalling can now be used to show that the marginals on the first factor
1786-are independent of the choice of measurement on the second.

1929-10. Postlude
1930-
--
1943-      and contextuality in physics, and ideas arising in other fields.
1944-
1945-   · The sheaf-theoretic language, which directly captures the idea of structures varying over
1946-      contexts, is a canonical setting for studying contextuality. Moreover, as we have seen, the
1947:      gluing conditions and the existence of global sections captures the essential content of non-
1948-      locality and contextuality in a canonical mathematical form.
1949-      This opens the door to the use of the powerful methods of sheaf theory, which plays a major
1950-      r^ole in modern mathematics, in analyzing the structure of non-locality and contextuality.
1951-      These notions are still poorly understood in multipartite and higher-dimensional settings.
1952-      In [53], the first author, with Shane Mansfield and Rui Soares Barbosa, define an abelian
1953:      presheaf based on the support of an empirical model. The C ech cohomology of this presheaf
1954:      with respect to the measurement cover is used to define a cohomological obstruction to locality
1955-      or non-contextuality, as a certain cohomology class. It is shown for a number of salient
1956-      examples, including PR boxes, GHZ states, the Peres-Mermin square, and the 18-vector
1957-      configuration from [21] giving a proof of the Kochen-Specker theorem in four dimensions,
1958-      that this obstruction does not vanish, thus yielding cohomological witnesses for contextuality.
--
1961-
1962-   · The canonical form of description of the key concepts in terms of the existence of global
1963-      sections largely replaces any explicit mention of hidden variables. These appear only in
1964-      Section 8, in the context of a foundational result showing the equivalence of local hidden-
1965:      variable realizations to the existence of global sections. On the other hand, empirical models,
1966-      which can be seen as directly related to observation and experiment, play a prominent r^ole
1967-      throughout the paper.
1968-
1969-      There is also an interesting conceptual point to be made in relation to incompatibility of
--
2004-with state [50, 51], and in the presheaf models for concurrency of Cattani and Winskel [52].
2005-
2006-      A more specific source of inspiration is the important insight in [57], which initiated the whole
2007-topos approach, that the Kochen-Specker theorem could be reformulated very elegantly in presheaf
2008:terms, as stating the non-existence of global sections of a certain presheaf.
2009-
2010-      On the other hand, there are several differences between the present work and the topos
2011-approach. For example, the topos approach focusses on a specific structure, the spectral presheaf,
2012-based on an operator algebra. In this sense, it uses concepts specific to quantum mechanics
2013-from the very start. Moreover, many of the key structures introduced in our work, such as the
2014:distribution functor and measurement covers, do not appear in the topos approach. One of our
2015-central objectives is to give a unified account of contextuality and non-locality, but locality issues
2016-have not been considered in the topos approach; nor has extendability, another key topic for us.
2017-It will, of course, be interesting to see if additional commonalities develop in future work.

  295: on X. In the case of the booleans B, it is the set of non-empty finite subsets of X; thus possibilistic
  296: or relational models [18, 19] are also covered. In the case of the reals R, it is the set of signed
  297: measures with finite support, allowing for `negative probabilities' [13, 14, 15, 16].
  298: 
  299:       Given a function f : X  Y , we define
  300: 
  301: DR(f ) : DR(X)  DR(Y ) :: d  [y                          d(x)].
  302: 
  303:                                                 f (x)=y
  304: 
  305: This is easily seen to be functorial:
  306: 
  307: DR(g  f ) = DR(g)  DR(f ),                      DR(idX ) = idDR(X)
  308: 
  309: so we have a functor DR : Set - Set.
  310:       We can compose this functor with the event sheaf E : P(X)op - Set, to form a presheaf
  311: 
  312: DRE : P(X)op - Set, which assigns to each set of measurements U the set DR(E(U )) of
  313: 
  314: distributions on U -sections. It is worth writing out the functorial action of this presheaf explicitly.
  315: Given U  U  we have a map
  316: 
  317: DRE(U )  DRE(U ) :: d  d|U,
  318: 
  319: where for each s  E(U ):
  320: 
  321: d|U (s) :=                               d(s).
  322: 
  323:                           sE(U ),s|U =s
  324: 
  325: Thus d|U is the marginal of the distribution d, which assigns to each section s in the smaller
  326: context U the sum of the weights of all sections s in the larger context which restrict to s.
  327: 
  328: 2.4. Measurement Covers
  329: 
  330: A crucial point is that it may not be possible, in general, to perform all measurements together.
  396: 
  397: We shall now show how the intuitive scenario described at the beginning of this section can be
  398: captured formally, using the mathematical structure we have developed.
  399: 
  400:       Suppose we are given a measurement cover M. Recall that M covers X, i.e. M = X.
  401:       We shall define a no-signalling empirical model for M to be a compatible family for
  402: the cover M with respect to the presheaf DRE. This means that for each measurement context
  403: C  M, there is a distribution eC  DRE(C). Moreover, this family of distributions is compatible
  404: in the sense of the sheaf condition: for all C, C  M,
  405: 
  406: eC|C  C = eC |C  C.
  407: 
  408: In the case of Bell-type scenarios, this is readily seen to coincide with the usual notion of no-
  409: signalling. For example, in the bipartite case, consider contexts C = {ma, mb}, C = {ma, mb},
  410: with a choice of measurement each for Alice and Bob. Fix s0  E({ma}), which assigns some
  411: 
  412: outcome to ma. Then the compatibility condition implies that
  413: 
  414:                        eC(s) =                       eC (s).
  415: 
  416: sE (C ),s|ma =s0                s E (C  ),s |ma =s0
  417: 
  418: This says that the probability for Alice to get the outcome specified by s0 for her measurement
  419: ma is the same, whether we marginalize over the possible outcomes for Bob when he makes the
  420: measurement mb, or the measurement mb . In other words, Bob's choice of measurement cannot
  421: influence Alice's outcome. This is exactly the standard definition of no-signalling.
  422: 
  423:       We should also note, as a boundary case, that E() is a one-element set, and DRE() is
  424: 
  425: again a one-element set. Thus if contexts have empty intersection, the compatibility condition is
  426: 
  427: trivially satisfied.
  428: The Sheaf-Theoretic Structure Of Non-Locality and Contextuality       8
  429: 
  430:       The general notion of compatible family for arbitrary covers M applies to a much wider range
  431: of situations than Bell-type scenarios; later we will show that the empirical models which can be
  432: represented as quantum mechanical systems satisfy this more general form of no-signalling.
  433: 
  434:       We shall only consider no-signalling models in this paper, so henceforth we shall simply speak
  435: of empirical models.

Learning Collective Variables with Synthetic Data Augmentation through Physics-Inspired Geodesic Interpolation
Soojung Yang
Juno Nam
Johannes C. B. Dietschreit
Rafael Gómez-Bombarelli
In molecular dynamics simulations, rare events, such as protein folding, are typically studied using enhanced sampling techniques, most of which are based on the definition of a collective variable (CV) along which acceleration occurs. Obtaining an expressive CV is crucial, but often hindered by the lack of information about the particular event, e.g., the transition from unfolded to folded conformation. We propose a simulation-free data augmentation strategy using physics-inspired metrics to generate geodesic interpolations resembling protein folding transitions, thereby improving sampling efficiency without true transition state samples. This new data can be used to improve the accuracy of classifier-based methods. Alternatively, a regression-based learning scheme for CV models can be adopted by leveraging the interpolation progress parameter.

The bridge fails in the only form that would answer the referee. Every support presheaf does have a canonical functorial split stack, but its component gerbes are neutral and carry zero \(H^2\)-classes. More decisively, AMB attaches a relative \(\check H^1\)-class to a chosen local section, while this paper attaches an \(H^2\)-class only to a global section of the sheafified component presheaf; for strongly contextual models that latter indexing set is empty precisely where AMB may be nonzero. I’m checking this against later contextuality literature before writing the negative theorem and transfer limits.

11-        Recent work by Abramsky and Brandenburger used sheaf theory to give a mathematical formulation
12-        of non-locality and contextuality. By adopting this viewpoint, it has been possible to define cohomo-
13:        logical obstructions to the existence of global sections. In the present work, we illustrate new insights
14-        into different aspects of this theory. We shed light on the power of detection of the cohomological
15-        obstruction by showing that it is not a complete invariant for strong contextuality even under symme-
16-        try and connectedness restrictions on the measurement cover, disproving a previous conjecture. We
17:        generalise obstructions to higher cohomology groups and show that they give rise to a refinement of
18-        the notion of cohomological contextuality: different "levels" of contextuality are organised in a hier-
19-        archy of logical implications. Finally, we present an alternative description of the first cohomology
20:        group in terms of torsors, resulting in a new interpretation of the cohomological obstructions.
21-
22-1 Introduction
23-
24-Contextuality is one of the most fundamental and peculiar features of quantum mechanics. Inspired by
--
30-various domains (e.g. relational databases [1] and constraint satisfaction [4]).
31-
32-    This rigorous mathematical formulation has allowed the application of powerful methods of sheaf
33-cohomology to the study of the topological structure of contextuality [2, 5]. Central to this approach
34:is the notion of cohomological obstruction to the existence of global sections, i.e. elements of the
35-first C ech cohomology group that provide a sufficient (but not necessary) condition for the contextuality
36-of empirical models. Although cohomology has been proved to correctly detect contextuality in various
37-well-studied empirical models such as PR boxes [25], GHZ states [12, 13, 20], the Peres-Mermin "magic"
38-square [22, 21, 24] and the whole class of models admitting "All-vs-Nothing" arguments [2] , there is
39:evidence of a restricted number of false positives (e.g. the Hardy model [15]).
40-
41:    In the present paper, we illustrate new insights into the properties of cohomological obstructions
42:with the ultimate goal of understanding how such false positives arise. In particular, we aim to give
43:an answer to some of the open questions left by [5]: "Is the cohomological obstruction a full invari-
44-ant for strong contextuality under suitable restrictions on the measurement scenario?"; "Can higher
45-cohomology groups be used for the study of contextuality?"; "Is there a concrete way of describing
46:cohomological obstructions?".

57-       which verifies any reasonably strong form of connectedness and symmetry condition.

59:    ˇ We generalise cohomological obstructions to higher cohomology groups. It turns out that this
60:       procedure can be done in a natural way only in odd dimensions. We obtain a refinement of the
61-       notion of cohomological contextuality: for each q  0, we say that a model is q-cohomologically
62-       contextual if the q-th obstruction does not vanish.

542-6 An alternative description of the first cohomology group
543-
544:Since higher cohomology groups cannot be used to infer information on how false positives arise, we
545-devote the last section of this paper to a detailed study of the first cohomology group H 1(M , FC~0). As
546-explained in [5], this group is of crucial importance for the cohomological study of contextuality, as it
547:contains all of the obstructions to the existence of global sections. Its relevance has been also previously
548-highlighted by Penrose in his On the cohomology of impossible figures [23], which presents "intriguing
549-resemblances" with our study [2]. Yet a full grasp of the nature of its elements is still to be achieved. We
550:propose here a description of H 1 based on the notion of F -torsors, as well as some considerations on
551-the connecting homomorphism .
552-
553-6.1 The connecting homomorphisms 
554-
555:The first step in understanding cohomological obstructions is studying the connecting homomorphisms.
556-We present here some insights on how the properties of  can give us information on the type of contex-
557-tuality of an empirical model.

563-sections s  F (C) and all contexts C  M . In other words, ker(C) = 0 for all C  M . For the converse,
564-suppose that ker(C) = 0 for all C  M . Then, every non-zero local section of F (C) has a non-zero
565:cohomological obstruction C(s). Thus the model is cohomologically strongly contextual.
566-
567-    Thanks to this result, we can give a lower bound for the cardinality of H 1(M , FC~0) in the case of
568-cohomologically strongly contextual models:
569-
570-                                       CSC(S )  |H 1(M , FC~0)|  |F (C0)|.
571-
572-On the other hand, given a CLC  ŹCSC model, Proposition 6.1 implies that two distinct sections may
573:give rise to the same non-zero cohomological obstruction.
574-
575-    The injectivity of a single connecting homomoprhism is a sufficient condition for the strong contex-
576-tuality of an empirical model.
577-
--
589-connecting homomorphisms {C}CM to be injective in order to conclude that a model is CSC, but it is
590-sufficient to have a single injective C to conclude that it is SC.
591-32  On the Cohomology of Contextuality
592-
593:6.2 F -torsors and their relation to H 1
594-
595:We start by recalling the main definitions; the reader not familiar with the concept of torsor relative to a
596-presheaf might refer to [27] for deeper insights. Let F : Open(X)op  AbGrp be a presheaf of abelian
597-groups over a topological space X. An F -presheaf is a presheaf of sets T over X equipped with a
598-morphism of presheaves  : F × T  T such that, for each open U  X, the map
599-
600-                  ˇ U : F (U) × T (U)  T (U) :: (g,t)  g t
601-
602-is a left action of F (U) on T (U). Given two F -presheaves T and T , a morphism of F -presheaves
603-from T to T is a morphism of presheaves  : T  T such that U is equivariant for all open U  X.
604:An F -presheaf T is called an F -torsor if
605-
606-   1. There exists an open cover V of X that trivialises T , i.e. such that T (V ) = 0/ for all V  V .
607-
608-   2. The action U : F (U) × T (U)  T (U) is simply transitive.
609:The simplest example of F -torsor is the trivial F -torsor U F ,9 where the action is simply given by
610:g.U (h) := U (g + h). We denote by TrsF the set of isomorphism classes of F -torsors. It can be proved
611:that an F -torsor T is isomorphic to the trivial F -torsor if and only if T (X) = 0/ .
612-
613-    Now, we adapt this discussion to the case of empirical models. Let F be an abelian presheaf repre-
614-senting an empirical model S on a scenario X, M , O , with M := {Ci}iI. Let
615-
616-                               Trs(M , F ) := {T  TrsF | T is trivialised by M } ,
617-
618:seen as a pointed set with the isomorphism class of the trivial F -torsor as distinguished element. We
619:have the following remarkable result, which is a readaptation of a known correspondence between torsors
620-and cohomology (the proof can be found in Appendix C).
621-Proposition 6.3. There is a bijection of pointed sets Trs(M , F ) = H 1(M , F ).
622-
623:    This bijection equips Trs(M , F ) with a group structure. The addition of two F -torsors is de-
624-fined componentwise at each subset U  X by g([z])(U) + g([w])(U) := g([z] + [w])(U) for all [z], [w] 
625-H 1(M , F ) (refer to Appendix C for the definition of the bijection g : H 1(M , F )  Trs(M , F )).
626-Clearly, the above bijection becomes an isomorphism of abelian groups with respect to this addition.
627-
628:    This results implies that the elements of the first cohomology group H 1(M , FC~0) relative to a context
629:C0  M (and, in particular, cohomological obstructions) can be seen as isomorphism classes of FC~0-
630:torsors trivialised by the measurement cover M .
631-
632-    Until now, elements of H 1 could only be identified via the abstract equations imposed by the rigid
633-definition of cohomology. The reason why we believe the new description might be more satisfactory,
634:is that despite their seemingly sophisticated definition, torsors are rather simple objects, as explained by
635:Baez in [6]. In the simplest terms, an FC~0-torsor is the presheaf FC~0 having lost its identity in each
636-group FC~0(U), for U  X. Rather than describing the local sections at each FC~0(U), it measures their
637-difference. We aim to further develop this viewpoint in future work.
638-
639-Conclusions
640-
641-Sheaf cohomology is a powerful method for the detection of contextuality. However, our work has high-
642-lighted some decisive limitations concerning C ech cohomology. Indeed, it cannot provide a full invariant
643-
644:    9Here, U : AbGrp  Set denotes the forgetful functor. To avoid confusion, we will not explicitly show its presence: the
645:trivial F -torsor will be simply denoted by F .
646-Giovanni Caru`  33
647-
648-for contextuality (neither logical nor strong) even under reasonably strong assumptions on symmetry and
649-connectedness of the cover, and, although obstructions can be generalised to higher cohomology groups,
--
653-inition of obstructions to the extension of continuous functions in a cohomology theory with coefficients
654-in the homotopy groups. This promising approach will require an adaptation of the concept of empiri-
655-cal model to fit this framework. A possibility would be to formalise the bundle diagram representation
656-and define models as fiber bundles or, more generally, as fibrations. This would allow the definition of
657:Postnikov towers [26], which give rise to cohomological obstructions.
658-
659-    In the last section, we have provided an alternative description of the first cohomology group using
660:torsors relative to a presheaf. Although this approach is still at a developing stage, it allows us to un-
661:derstand cohomological obstructions as a concrete mathematical object. The implications of this new
662-viewpoint will be considered in future work.

15-                                          of contextuality scenarios based on bundles of simplicial complexes and simplicial sets. The
16-                                          former approach generalizes earlier work on the sheaf-theoretic perspective on contextuality, and
17-                                          the latter extends simplicial distributions, a more recent approach to contextuality formulated
18-                                          in the language of simplicial sets. After constructing our bundle categories, we also construct
19:                                          functors that relate them and natural isomorphisms that allow us to compare the notions of
20-                                          contextuality formulated in two languages. We are motivated by applications to the resource
21-                                          theory of contextuality, captured by the morphisms in these categories. In this paper, we develop
22-                                          the main formalism and leave applications to future work.

85-1 Introduction
--
87-This paper develops a bundle perspective on contextuality that generalizes the sheaf-theoretic [1]
88-and the simplicial [2] approaches. In [3, 4], the former approach is used to construct the category
89-Scen of scenarios, whose morphisms capture a notion of simulation corresponding to the free
90-transformations in a resource theory of contextuality. In this paper, we introduce two categories: (1)
91:the category bScen of bundle scenarios based on simplicial complexes, and (2) the category sScen
92:of simplicial bundle scenarios based on simplicial sets. The use of bundles of simplicial complexes to
93-represent measurements and outcomes in contextuality scenarios already appears in the literature;
94-see [5­7]. However, the notion of "bundle" is used somewhat informally and not fully formalized.
95:We provide an abstract definition of a bundle scenario and define morphisms between such bundle
96-scenarios extending the category of scenarios Scen. The other category sScen is based on simplicial
97-sets, combinatorial objects representing spaces more expressive than simplicial complexes. Our
98-motivation for such extensions is to translate the resource-theoretic analysis developed in [3, 4, 8, 9]
99:to bundle scenarios of simplicial complexes and ultimately to bundle scenarios of simplicial sets.
100-The extension to simplicial sets carries many advantages for studying contextuality; see [2, 10­12].
101-It offers promising applications in extending cohomological frameworks for measurement-based
102-quantum computation developed in [13, 14].
103-
104-    This paper focuses on setting the formal stage, relating the three categories of scenarios and
105-distributions on them. Resource-theoretic implications will be studied in upcoming work. More
106:formally, we construct fully faithful functors
107-
108-                             E : Scen  bScen and N : bScen  sScen
109-
110-relating the three categories of scenarios and natural isomorphisms  and  relating the empirical

129-Each vertex x represents a measurement with outcomes in the set Ox, and each simplex   
130-represents a measurement context, a set of measurements that can be jointly performed. It is
131-convenient to represent the simplicial complex  as a category C whose objects are the simplices
132-of  and the morphisms are given by inclusions. Then both measurements and the corresponding
133:outcomes can be described as a functor
134-
135-                                                       EO : C  Set
136-
137-that sends a measurement context  to the set EO() = x Ox of all possible outcome assignments.
138:A morphism (, O)  (, O) between two scenarios consists of two parts: a functor  : C  C
139-induced by a simplicial relation that relates the measurement contexts, and a natural transformation
140- : EO    EO that specifies a mapping of outcomes over each context. Since measurements in
141-a context can be simultaneously performed, outcome statistics are represented by a probability
142-distribution e on the set EO() of joint outcomes. The family e = {e} of distributions, called
143:an empirical model, is required to satisfy an additional condition known as the non-signaling (or
144-no-disturbance) condition: the measurement statistics over two contexts should match on their
145:intersection. Morphisms of the category of scenarios are defined so that an empirical model e on
146:(, O) can be pushed forward along a morphism to produce a new empirical model on (, O).
147:Operationally this coincides with the notion of simulating the empirical model e with the new one.
148:By the push-forward construction, empirical models on scenarios can be turned into a functor
149-
150-                      Emp : Scen  Set
151-
152:Since we can consider probabilistic mixtures of empirical models, the target can be replaced by
153-the category ConvR of convex sets for our choice of a semiring R, which is usually taken to be
154-non-negative reals.

1262-
1263:In Sections 3 and 4 we have introduced distributions on scenarios of bundle scenarios based on

1267:empirical models and simplicial distributions. Our main result is Theorem 5.10 relating different
1268-versions of contextuality via these natural isomorphisms.

    1: \section{Concluding remarks}\label{sec:conclusion}
    2: 
    3: The paper separates three stages of the local-to-global problem. At the level of information states, \Cref{thm:pointwise-irreducibility} shows that compatible local sectionability and gluing-level nullity are invisible in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment considered here. This is not intended as a general expressivity theorem, but it does isolate the first place at which the local-object layer goes beyond the lower forcing language.
    4: 
    5: At the passage from set-valued to groupoid-valued data, \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} shows that a slice-separated representative-rigid lift can be globally conservative only when the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre is surjective; under $H^1$-vanishing and slice-separatedness on the reference slice, this is equivalent to sheafiness of the local object functor at that fibre. Thus the gerbe-theoretic part of the theory is necessarily relative to additional lift data. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} identifies the maximal canonicity available without an existence theorem: once the sheafified local object functor has been lifted to a banded realization stack, the branch obstruction class is intrinsic up to equivalence of such extensions. Visible value classes are then governed by the sheaf of connected components; on slice-separated reference slices, strict gluing failure is carried by the component gerbes of the visible branches.
    6: 
    7: For a finite abelian branch obstruction class, the presentation-object
    8: subgroup \(K_\omega=\operatorname{Im}(\mathrm{ev}_\omega)\) and quotient
    9: \(A_{\mathrm{vis}}^\omega=A/K_\omega\) capture the homological information
   10: that survives at a fixed finite nerve presentation; across presentations
   11: they form a groupoid-indexed invariant transported along chosen morphisms in
   12: the finite nerve comparison groupoid. The branchwise comparison sequence and
   13: the realization theorems show how these quotients behave when several
   14: visible branches are present, under the fixed finite nerve, constant-band,
   15: explicit \v{C}ech--derived comparison package, and \(H_1=0\) hypotheses used
   16: in the construction. When in addition
   17: \(H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^\beta\), the realizable hidden
   18: subgroups are exactly the subgroups generated by at most \(\beta\) elements.
   19: The bouquet construction supplies an explicit chosen class of good-cover
   20: examples in which the pure two-branch resolution kernels can be described
   21: completely: the nonzero finite abelian groups that occur are exactly those
   22: with \(d(G)\le2\beta\) which are not cyclic \(p\)-groups. The appendix
   23: contains only supplementary material: the refinement-dynamic extension,
   24: finite-state complexity bounds, and the GHZ/Mermin lift used as an
   25: illustrative chosen datum.
   26: 
   27: The hypothesis package is therefore deliberately visible: \textup{(RC)} for
   28: local objects, \textup{(H1)}--\textup{(H4)} and global conservativity for
   29: component gerbes, slice-separatedness whenever visible branches are used as
   30: strict compatible local sections, slice-separatedness and $H^1$-vanishing for
   31: terminal-fibre rigidity, and finite-nerve plus constant-band data together
   32: with the explicit \v{C}ech--derived comparison package for homological
   33: visibility.
   34: This paper keeps that package in the pullback-based slice-site formulation; the
   35: meet-semilattice presentation belongs to the companion APAL article. The
   36: comparison between presentations is consequently groupoid-indexed and
   37: zigzag-dependent, not a claim of presentation-free canonical representatives.
    1: \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
    2: 
    3: Sheaf-theoretic semantics offers a natural language for the passage from local data to global objects. In logical applications, and in particular in sheaf-theoretic analyses of contextuality \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,AbramskyBarbosaKishidaLalMansfield2015,Caru2017,Caru2018,Montanhano2021}, the central question is whether compatible local families glue to global sections. The classical tools for measuring the failure of gluing are gerbes, obstruction classes, and cohomological invariants \cite{Giraud1971,Breen2006,Hatcher2002}. In this paper we study that question in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations, with the aim of separating the successive layers at which genuinely new local-to-global structure appears.
    4: 
    5: Our starting point is the extension chain
    6: \[
    7: \mathbb{L}_0 \xhookrightarrow{\iota} \mathbb{L}_1 \preceq \mathbb{L}_2 \preceq \mathbb{L}_3 \preceq \mathbb{L}_4,
    8: \]
    9: where $\mathbb{L}_0$ is the pointwise layer, $\mathbb{L}_1$ is the information-state forcing layer, $\mathbb{L}_2$ adds local objects and site structure, $\mathbb{L}_3$ adds branchwise obstruction data, and $\mathbb{L}_4$ adds refinement dynamics. The map $\mathbb{L}_0\hookrightarrow\mathbb{L}_1$ is a singleton semantic embedding, whereas the later steps are conservative extensions in the sense of \Cref{def:conservative-extension}. Thus the geometric and homological material introduced later does not alter the forcing behaviour of formulas already present in the lower layers.
   10: The semantics is thus related both to team and imperfect-information semantics \cite{Hodges1997,Vaananen2007,AbramskyPuljujarviVaananen2025} and to the forcing and sheaf-theoretic tradition stemming from Beth, Kripke, Fitting, and Tierney and later developed in topos-theoretic form \cite{Beth1956,Kripke1965,Fitting1969,Tierney1972,Goldblatt2006,Johnstone2002}.
   11: 
   12: The first part of the paper concerns the passage from information states to local objects. \Cref{prop:compsec-to-sheafification} shows that compatible local sectionability gives nonemptiness of the associated sheafification, and \Cref{thm:sheafification-characterization} proves the converse on slice-separated reference slices. We then prove in \Cref{thm:pointwise-irreducibility} that the predicates $\CompSec_s$, $\Sec_s$, and $\Null^{\mathrm{glue}}_s$ are not definable by automorphism-invariant, constant-free formulas of the $\mathbb{L}_1$-reduct with one free reference variable. This is only a lower-bound statement for the comparison fragment under consideration, but it isolates a genuine change of behaviour between $\mathbb L_1$ and $\mathbb L_2$.
   13: 
   14: The second part begins once the set-valued local-object functor is enriched by groupoid-valued data. \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} gives a rigidity statement for representative-rigid lifts: if the local-object presheaf is slice-separated and a realization prestack admits a strict functorial choice of representatives and is globally conservative at the terminal fibre, then the sheafification unit is surjective there; under $H^1$-vanishing and the same slice-separatedness, this is equivalent to the local object functor already being a sheaf at the terminal fibre. Thus gluing-level nullity is necessarily tied to genuinely gluing-sensitive lift data. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} identifies the canonicity that survives at this level: once the sheafified local object functor has been lifted to a banded realization stack, the branch obstruction map to derived $H^2$ is intrinsic up to equivalence of banded extensions. For such an extension, visible value classes are the global sections of the sheaf of connected components (\Cref{thm:visible-value-components}), each visible branch determines a banded component gerbe (\Cref{thm:component-gerbe-decomposition}), and, on slice-separated reference slices, \Cref{thm:gerbe-null-semantics} identifies gluing-level absence with the existence of visible branches together with non-neutrality of the corresponding component gerbes. No general existence theorem for gluing-sensitive lifts is proved; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ghz} gives an explicit GHZ/Mermin example of chosen lift data.
   15: 
   16: The homological part of the paper starts only after one visible branch, one finite nerve presentation, and one constant finite abelian band have been fixed. From that point the tools are classical: the universal coefficient sequence, finite-abelian duality, and standard quotient arguments. What matters for the semantics, at a fixed presentation, is the presentation-object image
   17: \[
   18: K_\omega:=\operatorname{Im}(\mathrm{ev}_\omega)
   19: \]
   20: and quotient $A_{\mathrm{vis}}^\omega=A/K_\omega$ attached to the branch obstruction class. \Cref{prop:invariance-visible-quotients} establishes invariance under elementary homology-equivalent refinements, cocycle replacement, and re-trivialization of the band, and gives functorial transport along chosen finite comparison zigzags; it does not assert path independence between distinct zigzags. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-visible-quotient} gives the corresponding character-theoretic description, and \Cref{thm:character-blind-obstructions} identifies the character-blind case with the pure $\operatorname{Ext}$ contribution.
   21: 
   22: When several visible branches are present, one obtains branch-sensitive and branch-uniform quotients, related by the short exact sequence of \Cref{thm:branch-comparison-exact-sequence}. On a generated pullback subsite for a fixed finite nerve, with constant finite abelian band, the explicit finite-site Leray comparison of \Cref{lem:generated-subsite-model-interface}, and the additional assumption $H_1(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\allowbreak=0$, we prove realization theorems for prescribed branchwise homomorphisms $H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\allowbreak\to A$. These theorems are internal constructions under the generated admissible-expansion convention of \Cref{prop:admissible-layer-expansion-interface}: the algebraic data are built first, and the one-state $\mathbb L_2$- and $\mathbb L_3$-models are then obtained by admissible expansion. \Cref{thm:prescribed-branch-realization} treats non-neutral branches, while \Cref{thm:mixed-branch-realization} allows arbitrary finite families and identifies the neutral branches with the zero maps.
   23: 
   24: Under the same fixed finite-nerve, constant-band, $H_1=0$, and mixed-realization hypotheses, if $H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\cong \mathbb Z^\beta$, \Cref{cor:torsion-free-h2-classification} shows that the realizable hidden subgroups are exactly the subgroups of $A$ generated by at most $\beta$ elements. The bouquet theorem \Cref{thm:bouquet-two-branch-resolution} then supplies an explicit chosen family of examples, namely open-star good covers of a fixed finite model of $\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2$, for which the acyclic-cover hypothesis is automatic and the pure two-branch resolution kernels can be classified explicitly: a finite abelian group $G$ occurs precisely when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group. This is an existence and classification statement inside the chosen good-cover construction, not a uniqueness assertion for all presentations of the bouquet. In the unique-branch case this yields a direct comparison with the usual no-global-section picture from sheaf-theoretic contextuality; see \Cref{thm:unique-branch-contextuality-comparison}.
   25: 
   26: The sheaf-theoretic, gerbe-theoretic, and homological tools used here are classical, and several of the later comparison results are formal once the branchwise intrinsic data have been fixed. The contribution of the paper is accordingly structural: the extension chain separates the semantic layers, the dependence on extra realization data is made explicit, and the obstruction class gives rise to a groupoid-indexed invariant at fixed finite nerve presentations, with functorial transport along chosen finite comparison zigzags inside the controlled finite-nerve comparison groupoid.
   27: 
   28: The paper is organized as follows. \Cref{sec:preliminaries} fixes the extension chain and the relevant notions of conservativity. \Cref{sec:information-states} recalls forcing over information states. \Cref{sec:null-decomposition} studies local objects, sheafification, and lower-fragment separation. \Cref{sec:gerbe-obstruction} introduces component gerbes and branch obstruction classes. \Cref{sec:homological-visibility} and \Cref{sec:branch-aggregation} contain the homological visibility theory together with the branchwise comparison and realization results. The appendix collects the supplementary material on refinement dynamics and the GHZ/Mermin example.

   58: \title[Gluing Obstructions and Homological Visibility]{Gluing Obstructions and Homological Visibility in a State-Forcing Semantics}
   59: \author{Haobo Ma}
   60: \address[Haobo Ma]{AELF PTE LTD., \#14-02, Marina Bay Financial Centre Tower 1, 8 Marina Blvd, Singapore 018981}

   69: \begin{abstract}
   70: We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct. At the groupoid-valued level, representative rigidity and global conservativity force surjectivity of the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre; with $H^1$-vanishing this is equivalent to the local object functor already being a sheaf there. Hence gluing-level nullity cannot be recovered from a strict functorial choice of local representatives. For banded realization-stack extensions, each visible branch determines a canonical Giraud class in $H^2$. For finite abelian bands this yields a homological evaluation map whose image controls a presentation-object visible-quotient invariant, while the character-blind case is exactly the pure $\operatorname{Ext}$ contribution. On fixed finite nerves with $H_1=0$ and $H_2\cong\mathbb Z^\beta$, mixed realizations produce precisely the hidden subgroups generated by at most $\beta$ elements; on bouquet good covers, a nonzero finite abelian group occurs as a pure two-branch resolution kernel exactly when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group.
   71: \end{abstract}
   72:

12-        of non-locality and contextuality. By adopting this viewpoint, it has been possible to define cohomo-
13-        logical obstructions to the existence of global sections. In the present work, we illustrate new insights
14-        into different aspects of this theory. We shed light on the power of detection of the cohomological
15-        obstruction by showing that it is not a complete invariant for strong contextuality even under symme-
16-        try and connectedness restrictions on the measurement cover, disproving a previous conjecture. We
17-        generalise obstructions to higher cohomology groups and show that they give rise to a refinement of
18-        the notion of cohomological contextuality: different "levels" of contextuality are organised in a hier-
19-        archy of logical implications. Finally, we present an alternative description of the first cohomology
20:        group in terms of torsors, resulting in a new interpretation of the cohomological obstructions.

22-1 Introduction
23-
24-Contextuality is one of the most fundamental and peculiar features of quantum mechanics. Inspired by
25-classic no-go theorems by Bell [9] and Kochen-Specker [17], the development of quantum information
26-has been increasingly influenced by the study of this highly non-classical phenomenon. Recent work by
27-Howard et al. has even suggested that it actually represents the source of the power of quantum computing
28-[16]. The sheaf-theoretic description of non-locality and contextuality introduced in [3] has proved that
--
62-       contextual if the q-th obstruction does not vanish.
63-
64-    � We show that higher obstructions are organised in a precise hierarchy of logical implications.
65-       We also prove that, unfortunately, this result cannot be used in the study of contextuality in no-
66-       signalling empirical models. Despite this fact, higher obstructions could potentially be used to
67-       study signalling properties.
68-
69-    � We give a new description of the first cohomology group (thus, in particular, of the cohomology
70:       obstructions) using torsors relative to a presheaf.
71-
72-    The paper is organised as follows. We summarise the sheaf viewpoint from [3] in Section 2, and recall
73-the main definitions concerning sheaf cohomology in Section 3. Section 4 features the counterexample
74-to Conjecture 8.1 of [5]. We generalise cohomological obstructions to higher cohomology groups in
75:Section 5. Finally, in Section 6, we present torsors relative to a presheaf, and their relation to the first
76-sheaf cohomology group.

78-2 The sheaf-theoretic framework
79-
80-In this section we recall the main definitions of the sheaf-theoretic approach to non-locality and contex-
81-tuality [3].
82-
83-    We start by considering a finite discrete space X, which can be seen as a set of measurement labels.
--
542-6 An alternative description of the first cohomology group
543-
544-Since higher cohomology groups cannot be used to infer information on how false positives arise, we
545-devote the last section of this paper to a detailed study of the first cohomology group H 1(M , FC~0). As
546-explained in [5], this group is of crucial importance for the cohomological study of contextuality, as it
547-contains all of the obstructions to the existence of global sections. Its relevance has been also previously
548-highlighted by Penrose in his On the cohomology of impossible figures [23], which presents "intriguing
549-resemblances" with our study [2]. Yet a full grasp of the nature of its elements is still to be achieved. We
550:propose here a description of H 1 based on the notion of F -torsors, as well as some considerations on
551-the connecting homomorphism .
552-

554-
555-The first step in understanding cohomological obstructions is studying the connecting homomorphisms.
556-We present here some insights on how the properties of  can give us information on the type of contex-
557-tuality of an empirical model.

593:6.2 F -torsors and their relation to H 1
594-
595:We start by recalling the main definitions; the reader not familiar with the concept of torsor relative to a
596-presheaf might refer to [27] for deeper insights. Let F : Open(X)op  AbGrp be a presheaf of abelian
597-groups over a topological space X. An F -presheaf is a presheaf of sets T over X equipped with a
598-morphism of presheaves  : F � T  T such that, for each open U  X, the map
599-
600-                  � U : F (U) � T (U)  T (U) :: (g,t)  g t
601-
602-is a left action of F (U) on T (U). Given two F -presheaves T and T , a morphism of F -presheaves
603-from T to T is a morphism of presheaves  : T  T such that U is equivariant for all open U  X.
604:An F -presheaf T is called an F -torsor if
605-
606-   1. There exists an open cover V of X that trivialises T , i.e. such that T (V ) = 0/ for all V  V .
607-
608-   2. The action U : F (U) � T (U)  T (U) is simply transitive.
609:The simplest example of F -torsor is the trivial F -torsor U F ,9 where the action is simply given by
610:g.U (h) := U (g + h). We denote by TrsF the set of isomorphism classes of F -torsors. It can be proved
611:that an F -torsor T is isomorphic to the trivial F -torsor if and only if T (X) = 0/ .
612-
613-    Now, we adapt this discussion to the case of empirical models. Let F be an abelian presheaf repre-
614-senting an empirical model S on a scenario X, M , O , with M := {Ci}iI. Let
615-
616:                               Trs(M , F ) := {T  TrsF | T is trivialised by M } ,
617-
618:seen as a pointed set with the isomorphism class of the trivial F -torsor as distinguished element. We
619:have the following remarkable result, which is a readaptation of a known correspondence between torsors
620-and cohomology (the proof can be found in Appendix C).
621:Proposition 6.3. There is a bijection of pointed sets Trs(M , F ) = H 1(M , F ).
622-
623:    This bijection equips Trs(M , F ) with a group structure. The addition of two F -torsors is de-
624-fined componentwise at each subset U  X by g([z])(U) + g([w])(U) := g([z] + [w])(U) for all [z], [w] 
625:H 1(M , F ) (refer to Appendix C for the definition of the bijection g : H 1(M , F )  Trs(M , F )).
626:Clearly, the above bijection becomes an isomorphism of abelian groups with respect to this addition.
627-
628-    This results implies that the elements of the first cohomology group H 1(M , FC~0) relative to a context
629-C0  M (and, in particular, cohomological obstructions) can be seen as isomorphism classes of FC~0-
630:torsors trivialised by the measurement cover M .
631-
632-    Until now, elements of H 1 could only be identified via the abstract equations imposed by the rigid
633-definition of cohomology. The reason why we believe the new description might be more satisfactory,
634:is that despite their seemingly sophisticated definition, torsors are rather simple objects, as explained by
635:Baez in [6]. In the simplest terms, an FC~0-torsor is the presheaf FC~0 having lost its identity in each
636-group FC~0(U), for U  X. Rather than describing the local sections at each FC~0(U), it measures their
637-difference. We aim to further develop this viewpoint in future work.
638-
639-Conclusions
640-
641-Sheaf cohomology is a powerful method for the detection of contextuality. However, our work has high-
642-lighted some decisive limitations concerning C ech cohomology. Indeed, it cannot provide a full invariant
643-
644-    9Here, U : AbGrp  Set denotes the forgetful functor. To avoid confusion, we will not explicitly show its presence: the
645:trivial F -torsor will be simply denoted by F .
646-Giovanni Caru`  33
647-
648-for contextuality (neither logical nor strong) even under reasonably strong assumptions on symmetry and
649-connectedness of the cover, and, although obstructions can be generalised to higher cohomology groups,
650-they cannot be applied to the study of no-signalling empirical models. In future work, we aim to re-
651-develop the sheaf-cohomological study of contextuality from a different viewpoint. The machinery of
652-obstruction theory, a branch of homotopy theory that deals with the extendability of maps, allows the def-
653-inition of obstructions to the extension of continuous functions in a cohomology theory with coefficients
654-in the homotopy groups. This promising approach will require an adaptation of the concept of empiri-
655-cal model to fit this framework. A possibility would be to formalise the bundle diagram representation
656-and define models as fiber bundles or, more generally, as fibrations. This would allow the definition of
657-Postnikov towers [26], which give rise to cohomological obstructions.
658-
659-    In the last section, we have provided an alternative description of the first cohomology group using
660:torsors relative to a presheaf. Although this approach is still at a developing stage, it allows us to un-
661-derstand cohomological obstructions as a concrete mathematical object. The implications of this new
662-viewpoint will be considered in future work.

12-                                                                                                  Abstract
13-
14:                                              This paper provides a bundle perspective to contextuality by introducing new categories
15:                                          of contextuality scenarios based on bundles of simplicial complexes and simplicial sets. The
16:                                          former approach generalizes earlier work on the sheaf-theoretic perspective on contextuality, and
17:                                          the latter extends simplicial distributions, a more recent approach to contextuality formulated
18:                                          in the language of simplicial sets. After constructing our bundle categories, we also construct
19-                                          functors that relate them and natural isomorphisms that allow us to compare the notions of
20:                                          contextuality formulated in two languages. We are motivated by applications to the resource
21:                                          theory of contextuality, captured by the morphisms in these categories. In this paper, we develop
22-                                          the main formalism and leave applications to future work.

85-1 Introduction
86-
87:This paper develops a bundle perspective on contextuality that generalizes the sheaf-theoretic [1]
88-and the simplicial [2] approaches. In [3, 4], the former approach is used to construct the category
89-Scen of scenarios, whose morphisms capture a notion of simulation corresponding to the free
90:transformations in a resource theory of contextuality. In this paper, we introduce two categories: (1)
91:the category bScen of bundle scenarios based on simplicial complexes, and (2) the category sScen
92:of simplicial bundle scenarios based on simplicial sets. The use of bundles of simplicial complexes to
93:represent measurements and outcomes in contextuality scenarios already appears in the literature;
94:see [5�7]. However, the notion of "bundle" is used somewhat informally and not fully formalized.
95:We provide an abstract definition of a bundle scenario and define morphisms between such bundle
96-scenarios extending the category of scenarios Scen. The other category sScen is based on simplicial
97-sets, combinatorial objects representing spaces more expressive than simplicial complexes. Our
98-motivation for such extensions is to translate the resource-theoretic analysis developed in [3, 4, 8, 9]
99:to bundle scenarios of simplicial complexes and ultimately to bundle scenarios of simplicial sets.
100:The extension to simplicial sets carries many advantages for studying contextuality; see [2, 10�12].
101:It offers promising applications in extending cohomological frameworks for measurement-based
102-quantum computation developed in [13, 14].
103-
104-    This paper focuses on setting the formal stage, relating the three categories of scenarios and
105-distributions on them. Resource-theoretic implications will be studied in upcoming work. More
106-formally, we construct fully faithful functors

154-non-negative reals.

12-                                                                                                  Abstract
13-
14:                                              This paper provides a bundle perspective to contextuality by introducing new categories
15:                                          of contextuality scenarios based on bundles of simplicial complexes and simplicial sets. The
16:                                          former approach generalizes earlier work on the sheaf-theoretic perspective on contextuality, and
17:                                          the latter extends simplicial distributions, a more recent approach to contextuality formulated
18:                                          in the language of simplicial sets. After constructing our bundle categories, we also construct
19-                                          functors that relate them and natural isomorphisms that allow us to compare the notions of
20:                                          contextuality formulated in two languages. We are motivated by applications to the resource
21:                                          theory of contextuality, captured by the morphisms in these categories. In this paper, we develop
22-                                          the main formalism and leave applications to future work.

    1: \section{Concluding remarks}\label{sec:conclusion}
    2: 
    3: The paper separates three stages of the local-to-global problem. At the level of information states, \Cref{thm:pointwise-irreducibility} shows that compatible local sectionability and gluing-level nullity are invisible in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment considered here. This is not intended as a general expressivity theorem, but it does isolate the first place at which the local-object layer goes beyond the lower forcing language.
    4: 
    5: At the passage from set-valued to groupoid-valued data, \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} shows that a slice-separated representative-rigid lift can be globally conservative only when the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre is surjective; under $H^1$-vanishing and slice-separatedness on the reference slice, this is equivalent to sheafiness of the local object functor at that fibre. Thus the gerbe-theoretic part of the theory is necessarily relative to additional lift data. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} identifies the maximal canonicity available without an existence theorem: once the sheafified local object functor has been lifted to a banded realization stack, the branch obstruction class is intrinsic up to equivalence of such extensions. Visible value classes are then governed by the sheaf of connected components; on slice-separated reference slices, strict gluing failure is carried by the component gerbes of the visible branches.
    6: 
    7: For a finite abelian branch obstruction class, the presentation-object
    8: subgroup \(K_\omega=\operatorname{Im}(\mathrm{ev}_\omega)\) and quotient
    9: \(A_{\mathrm{vis}}^\omega=A/K_\omega\) capture the homological information
   10: that survives at a fixed finite nerve presentation; across presentations
   11: they form a groupoid-indexed invariant transported along chosen morphisms in
   12: the finite nerve comparison groupoid. The branchwise comparison sequence and
   13: the realization theorems show how these quotients behave when several
   14: visible branches are present, under the fixed finite nerve, constant-band,
   15: explicit \v{C}ech--derived comparison package, and \(H_1=0\) hypotheses used
   16: in the construction. When in addition
   17: \(H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^\beta\), the realizable hidden
   18: subgroups are exactly the subgroups generated by at most \(\beta\) elements.
   19: The bouquet construction supplies an explicit chosen class of good-cover
   20: examples in which the pure two-branch resolution kernels can be described
   21: completely: the nonzero finite abelian groups that occur are exactly those
   22: with \(d(G)\le2\beta\) which are not cyclic \(p\)-groups. The appendix
   23: contains only supplementary material: the refinement-dynamic extension,
   24: finite-state complexity bounds, and the GHZ/Mermin lift used as an
   25: illustrative chosen datum.
   26: 
   27: The hypothesis package is therefore deliberately visible: \textup{(RC)} for
   28: local objects, \textup{(H1)}--\textup{(H4)} and global conservativity for
   29: component gerbes, slice-separatedness whenever visible branches are used as
   30: strict compatible local sections, slice-separatedness and $H^1$-vanishing for
   31: terminal-fibre rigidity, and finite-nerve plus constant-band data together
   32: with the explicit \v{C}ech--derived comparison package for homological
   33: visibility.
   34: This paper keeps that package in the pullback-based slice-site formulation; the
   35: meet-semilattice presentation belongs to the companion APAL article. The
   36: comparison between presentations is consequently groupoid-indexed and
   37: zigzag-dependent, not a claim of presentation-free canonical representatives.
    1: \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
    2: 
    3: Sheaf-theoretic semantics offers a natural language for the passage from local data to global objects. In logical applications, and in particular in sheaf-theoretic analyses of contextuality \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,AbramskyBarbosaKishidaLalMansfield2015,Caru2017,Caru2018,Montanhano2021}, the central question is whether compatible local families glue to global sections. The classical tools for measuring the failure of gluing are gerbes, obstruction classes, and cohomological invariants \cite{Giraud1971,Breen2006,Hatcher2002}. In this paper we study that question in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations, with the aim of separating the successive layers at which genuinely new local-to-global structure appears.
    4: 
    5: Our starting point is the extension chain
    6: \[
    7: \mathbb{L}_0 \xhookrightarrow{\iota} \mathbb{L}_1 \preceq \mathbb{L}_2 \preceq \mathbb{L}_3 \preceq \mathbb{L}_4,
    8: \]
    9: where $\mathbb{L}_0$ is the pointwise layer, $\mathbb{L}_1$ is the information-state forcing layer, $\mathbb{L}_2$ adds local objects and site structure, $\mathbb{L}_3$ adds branchwise obstruction data, and $\mathbb{L}_4$ adds refinement dynamics. The map $\mathbb{L}_0\hookrightarrow\mathbb{L}_1$ is a singleton semantic embedding, whereas the later steps are conservative extensions in the sense of \Cref{def:conservative-extension}. Thus the geometric and homological material introduced later does not alter the forcing behaviour of formulas already present in the lower layers.
   10: The semantics is thus related both to team and imperfect-information semantics \cite{Hodges1997,Vaananen2007,AbramskyPuljujarviVaananen2025} and to the forcing and sheaf-theoretic tradition stemming from Beth, Kripke, Fitting, and Tierney and later developed in topos-theoretic form \cite{Beth1956,Kripke1965,Fitting1969,Tierney1972,Goldblatt2006,Johnstone2002}.
   11: 
   12: The first part of the paper concerns the passage from information states to local objects. \Cref{prop:compsec-to-sheafification} shows that compatible local sectionability gives nonemptiness of the associated sheafification, and \Cref{thm:sheafification-characterization} proves the converse on slice-separated reference slices. We then prove in \Cref{thm:pointwise-irreducibility} that the predicates $\CompSec_s$, $\Sec_s$, and $\Null^{\mathrm{glue}}_s$ are not definable by automorphism-invariant, constant-free formulas of the $\mathbb{L}_1$-reduct with one free reference variable. This is only a lower-bound statement for the comparison fragment under consideration, but it isolates a genuine change of behaviour between $\mathbb L_1$ and $\mathbb L_2$.
   13: 
   14: The second part begins once the set-valued local-object functor is enriched by groupoid-valued data. \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} gives a rigidity statement for representative-rigid lifts: if the local-object presheaf is slice-separated and a realization prestack admits a strict functorial choice of representatives and is globally conservative at the terminal fibre, then the sheafification unit is surjective there; under $H^1$-vanishing and the same slice-separatedness, this is equivalent to the local object functor already being a sheaf at the terminal fibre. Thus gluing-level nullity is necessarily tied to genuinely gluing-sensitive lift data. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} identifies the canonicity that survives at this level: once the sheafified local object functor has been lifted to a banded realization stack, the branch obstruction map to derived $H^2$ is intrinsic up to equivalence of banded extensions. For such an extension, visible value classes are the global sections of the sheaf of connected components (\Cref{thm:visible-value-components}), each visible branch determines a banded component gerbe (\Cref{thm:component-gerbe-decomposition}), and, on slice-separated reference slices, \Cref{thm:gerbe-null-semantics} identifies gluing-level absence with the existence of visible branches together with non-neutrality of the corresponding component gerbes. No general existence theorem for gluing-sensitive lifts is proved; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ghz} gives an explicit GHZ/Mermin example of chosen lift data.
   15: 
   16: The homological part of the paper starts only after one visible branch, one finite nerve presentation, and one constant finite abelian band have been fixed. From that point the tools are classical: the universal coefficient sequence, finite-abelian duality, and standard quotient arguments. What matters for the semantics, at a fixed presentation, is the presentation-object image
   17: \[
   18: K_\omega:=\operatorname{Im}(\mathrm{ev}_\omega)
   19: \]
   20: and quotient $A_{\mathrm{vis}}^\omega=A/K_\omega$ attached to the branch obstruction class. \Cref{prop:invariance-visible-quotients} establishes invariance under elementary homology-equivalent refinements, cocycle replacement, and re-trivialization of the band, and gives functorial transport along chosen finite comparison zigzags; it does not assert path independence between distinct zigzags. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-visible-quotient} gives the corresponding character-theoretic description, and \Cref{thm:character-blind-obstructions} identifies the character-blind case with the pure $\operatorname{Ext}$ contribution.
   21: 
   22: When several visible branches are present, one obtains branch-sensitive and branch-uniform quotients, related by the short exact sequence of \Cref{thm:branch-comparison-exact-sequence}. On a generated pullback subsite for a fixed finite nerve, with constant finite abelian band, the explicit finite-site Leray comparison of \Cref{lem:generated-subsite-model-interface}, and the additional assumption $H_1(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\allowbreak=0$, we prove realization theorems for prescribed branchwise homomorphisms $H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\allowbreak\to A$. These theorems are internal constructions under the generated admissible-expansion convention of \Cref{prop:admissible-layer-expansion-interface}: the algebraic data are built first, and the one-state $\mathbb L_2$- and $\mathbb L_3$-models are then obtained by admissible expansion. \Cref{thm:prescribed-branch-realization} treats non-neutral branches, while \Cref{thm:mixed-branch-realization} allows arbitrary finite families and identifies the neutral branches with the zero maps.
   23: 
   24: Under the same fixed finite-nerve, constant-band, $H_1=0$, and mixed-realization hypotheses, if $H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\cong \mathbb Z^\beta$, \Cref{cor:torsion-free-h2-classification} shows that the realizable hidden subgroups are exactly the subgroups of $A$ generated by at most $\beta$ elements. The bouquet theorem \Cref{thm:bouquet-two-branch-resolution} then supplies an explicit chosen family of examples, namely open-star good covers of a fixed finite model of $\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2$, for which the acyclic-cover hypothesis is automatic and the pure two-branch resolution kernels can be classified explicitly: a finite abelian group $G$ occurs precisely when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group. This is an existence and classification statement inside the chosen good-cover construction, not a uniqueness assertion for all presentations of the bouquet. In the unique-branch case this yields a direct comparison with the usual no-global-section picture from sheaf-theoretic contextuality; see \Cref{thm:unique-branch-contextuality-comparison}.
   25: 
   26: The sheaf-theoretic, gerbe-theoretic, and homological tools used here are classical, and several of the later comparison results are formal once the branchwise intrinsic data have been fixed. The contribution of the paper is accordingly structural: the extension chain separates the semantic layers, the dependence on extra realization data is made explicit, and the obstruction class gives rise to a groupoid-indexed invariant at fixed finite nerve presentations, with functorial transport along chosen finite comparison zigzags inside the controlled finite-nerve comparison groupoid.
   27: 
   28: The paper is organized as follows. \Cref{sec:preliminaries} fixes the extension chain and the relevant notions of conservativity. \Cref{sec:information-states} recalls forcing over information states. \Cref{sec:null-decomposition} studies local objects, sheafification, and lower-fragment separation. \Cref{sec:gerbe-obstruction} introduces component gerbes and branch obstruction classes. \Cref{sec:homological-visibility} and \Cref{sec:branch-aggregation} contain the homological visibility theory together with the branchwise comparison and realization results. The appendix collects the supplementary material on refinement dynamics and the GHZ/Mermin example.

   69: \begin{abstract}
   70: We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct. At the groupoid-valued level, representative rigidity and global conservativity force surjectivity of the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre; with $H^1$-vanishing this is equivalent to the local object functor already being a sheaf there. Hence gluing-level nullity cannot be recovered from a strict functorial choice of local representatives. For banded realization-stack extensions, each visible branch determines a canonical Giraud class in $H^2$. For finite abelian bands this yields a homological evaluation map whose image controls a presentation-object visible-quotient invariant, while the character-blind case is exactly the pure $\operatorname{Ext}$ contribution. On fixed finite nerves with $H_1=0$ and $H_2\cong\mathbb Z^\beta$, mixed realizations produce precisely the hidden subgroups generated by at most $\beta$ elements; on bouquet good covers, a nonzero finite abelian group occurs as a pure two-branch resolution kernel exactly when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group.
   71: \end{abstract}

27-Howard et al. has even suggested that it actually represents the source of the power of quantum computing
28-[16]. The sheaf-theoretic description of non-locality and contextuality introduced in [3] has proved that
